translations.text: Abba Poemen said: A brother said to Abba Paesius, What should I do about my heart, since it is hard?
I do not fear God.
He said to him: Go and attach yourself to a brother who fears God, and through that brother’s fear of God, you too will fear God.
Someone asked an elder: Why does my heart wander everywhere while I sit in my cell?
The elder answered him: Because your outward senses are sick: seeing, hearing, smelling, and speaking.
If, then, you exercise these in purity, your inward senses become calm and healthy.
Someone else asked an elder: Why am I restless while I sit in my cell?
He answered him: Because you have not yet understood the rest we hope for, or the punishment that is to come.
If you had understood these things firmly, even if your cell were filled with thorns up to your neck, you would remain among them and endure them without becoming restless.
An elder saw someone laughing.
He said:
[?] Likewise, the chosen monk is among thoughts of desire.
He also said: Fasting is the monk’s bridle in his fight against sin.
Whoever throws it away is a horse mad with lust.
He also said: It is better to eat meat and drink wine than to eat your brothers’ flesh through slander.
On another occasion, they received a jar of wine as a firstfruits offering, to give the brothers one cup each.
One of the brothers went up onto the roof.
He ran away from it, and immediately the [?] fell.
They went to look because of the noise that had occurred.
They found the brother lying on the ground.
They began to insult him, saying: You are a lover of empty glory.
It serves you right that this happened to you.
But the elder kissed him, saying:
Leave my son alone.
For what he did was a good thing.
As the Lord lives, this roof will not be rebuilt in my lifetime.
Let the whole world know that a vaulted roof collapsed in Scetis because of a cup of wine.
A brother was stirred to anger against someone.
He stood up to pray and asked to receive patience toward his brother and to overcome the temptation without harm.
Immediately he saw smoke coming out of his mouth.
When this happened, he stopped being angry.
Once the priest of Scetis went to the archbishop of Alexandria.
When he returned to Scetis, the brothers asked him, “How is the city?”
He said to them, “[?], my brothers, I did not see anyone’s face except the archbishop’s alone.”
When they heard this, they were strengthened by his words to guard themselves outwardly against letting their eyes wander.
An elder said, “The devil settles on a monk’s wounds. If a habit stays with him
for a long time, it becomes established and gains strength like a natural disposition, especially in those who are particularly careless.”
Do not give your belly all the foods you seek for it when it is hungry, especially when you are healthy rather than sick.
And do not eat what you crave.
Instead, eat what God has sent you, and thank him at all times.
We have consumed the monks’ bread and enjoyed all their comfort.
But we have not done the monks’ work.
Say to yourself alone, “Brother, keep for yourself the seal of Christ, which is humility.
One of the elders went to another elder and said to his disciple, “Prepare a little lentil gruel for us.”
And he prepared it.
He said, “Soak the bread for us,” and he soaked it.
But they continued talking about spiritual matters all day and all night.
But you are a worldly person; you do not have the strength to live in this place.”
Abba Isaac said, “Our fathers, including Abba Pambo, wore ragged tunics covered with patches, and tunics made of palm fiber.
But now you wear expensive tunics.
Leave this place.
You have ruined it.”
When they were going to the harvest, he said to them, “I will not go on [?] giving you instructions.
For you do not keep them.”
He also said, “Abba Pambo said, ‘This is how a monk ought to wear his clothes.’”
So he should throw his garment outside his cell for three days, and no one should think it worth picking up.
Then he may wear it.
Abba Cassian said that one of the senators spoke, having renounced all his possessions.
He gave them to the poor.
He kept a little for himself to meet his own needs.
He did not want to live in complete renunciation. On humility.
Basil [?], who is among the saints, said something to this man.
He said, “You have lost your status as a senator, and you have not attained the life of a monk.”
One of the brothers asked Abba Pistamon, “What should I do? People put pressure on me when I sell my handiwork.”
The old man answered, “Abba Sisoes and the others also sell their handiwork.
There is no harm in this.
But when you go to sell it, state the price just once and hand it over.
If you want to take a little off its price, you decide. This is how you will find rest.”
The brother said to him, “If I have what I need, do you want me not to concern myself with manual work?”
The old man answered, “Even if you have everything, do not give up manual work.
Do whatever you are able to do, but not with anxiety.”
A brother asked Abba Serapion, “Say a word to me.”
The old man said to him, “What am I to say to you?
You have taken the belongings of the poor, the widows, and the orphans and put them in the cupboard.”
For he had seen the cupboard full of books.
They asked the blessed Syncletica whether owning nothing was a perfect good.
She answered, “It is an especially perfect good for those who have no strength.
For those who endure this have affliction in the flesh, but grace in the soul.
Just as tough clothes are trampled on, wrung out, and vigorously turned until they become clean, so a soul that is strong in poverty imposed against its will becomes still stronger.”
A brother living alone in the cells became troubled. He went to Abba Theodore of Pherme and told him.
The elder said to him, “Go, humble your heart, and live with others, submitting to them.”
Then he went and stayed with some others on the mountain. He returned again and came to the old man.
He said, “I have found no rest living with other people.”
But the old man said to him, “If you have found no rest alone, you will not find rest living with others either.”
“Why did you leave to become a monk?
Was it not so that you would endure hardships?
Tell me, how many years has it been since you put on this monastic habit?”
He said, “It has been eight years.”
The old man said to him, “Indeed, it has been seventy years since I became a monk.”
“I have not found rest for a single day, and you want to rest during these eight years!”
They said of Abba Theodore and Abba Lucian of the Enaton that they spent fifty years deceiving their own thoughts, saying, “When winter is over, we will move away from this place.”
But when summer came, they would say, “When summer passes, we will move away from this place.”
And this is how our fathers, whose memory is celebrated forever, spent all that time.
Abba Macarius the Great went to Abba Anthony.
And when he knocked at the door, he came out to him and said to him, “Who are you?”
He answered, saying, “I am Macarius.”
And he shut the door, went inside, and left him.
But when he saw his perseverance, he opened the door for him
and greeted him joyfully, saying, “I have wanted to see you for a long time, for I have heard about you.”
And he welcomed him kindly and gave him rest, for he had come through great hardships.
When evening came, Abba Antony soaked a few palm leaves for himself.
Abba Macarius said to him, “Give me permission to soak some for myself.”
He said, “Soak some.”
And he made a large bundle of palm leaves and soaked it.
They sat and spoke about what benefits the soul.
They wove from evening onward, and the rope went down into the porch through the window.
In the morning, the blessed Abba Antony went inside and saw how much rope Abba Macarius had made.
He was amazed and kissed Abba Macarius’s hands, saying, “Many mighty works have come from these hands.”
The old man, Abba Macarius, once went from Scetis to Terenouthis.
And he went into a small place and lay down to sleep.
There were some [?] there.
of bitter pleasure.
These are the things about which they laid down rules for us.
But if illness has made us unable to do these things, the instruction is unnecessary.
But why do I say that the instruction is unnecessary?
For suffering that destroys sin has been provided like a powerful medicine that works effectively in the sick person's body.
And this is the great ascetic discipline: endurance in illnesses and thanksgiving through hymns, sending them up to God so that we may lift our eyes to him with thanksgiving.
Let us not be as though we were waking from sleep, for we have cast away from ourselves the instruments of intemperance.
But we see the glory of God as in a mirror through the inward eye of the heart, even if the eye of our outward body has been taken from us.
If we become deaf, let us give thanks because we have left behind listening to [?] worthless things.
We have become disabled [?].
We have [?] the things within us, ready for the enemy’s attack.
Even if illness has taken hold of our whole body, healing increases all the more in the inner person.
She also said, “In the world, those who are disabled are not thrown into prison.
They are protected from committing sin.
But as for our sins, let us examine ourselves on our own, so that by our own free choice we may cast away from ourselves the punishments that are to come.
When you fast, do not use illnesses as an excuse.
For others who do not fast also fall into these same afflictions.
You have begun to do good; do not turn back.
For the enemy is putting obstacles in your way.
[?] For he himself [?] was weakened through [?] endurance.
[?] those who have begun [?] to sail [?] a south wind [?]. They spread out their sail.
Afterward, the wind that opposes them strikes them. But the sailors do not unload the cargo because of the many winds that have come upon them.
They rest a little and continue struggling with the wave that has come upon them as they sail.
This is also our way.
If a strong wind opposes us, let us spread out the cross in place of the sail and complete the voyage without fear.”
They said about the blessed virgin Sarah that she lived for sixty years above the river, but never leaned out to look at the river.
Abba Hyperechius said, “Spiritual singing and constant meditation weaken the attacks that come upon us.”
He also said, “We ought to arm ourselves before temptation.
For they are coming.”
And if they come and find us keeping watch, we will receive glory.
An elder said, “When a trial rises against someone, troubles multiply for him on every side, so that he loses heart and grumbles.”
And the elder spoke as follows:
“There was a brother among the cells against whom a trial arose.
And whenever anyone saw him, he would not willingly greet him or bring him into his cell.
And when he needed bread, no one would lend him any.
And whenever he went out to the harvest, they would not invite him, nor even to the church, as though it were the Creator who invited them to the love feast.
But once he came back from the field,
and he had no bread in his cell.
And in all these things he would give thanks to God [?].
But God saw his endurance and removed it from him.”
[?] of this [?].
“I will come and live near the water.”
When he said this, he turned his face and saw someone following him, counting his footsteps.
He asked him, “Who are you?”
He said, “I am an angel of the Lord,
sent to count your footsteps and give you your reward.”
When the elder heard these things, his heart was comforted, and he became even more vigorous.
He added another five miles to the distance, farther into the desert.
The elders said, “If a trial rises against you in the place where you are, do not abandon your place during the trial.
Otherwise, in the place you go to, you will again find what you are fleeing from.
Instead, endure until the trial passes, so that your departure may be [?] a stumbling block, and in a time of peace, so that your departure may not become an affliction to those [?] in the [?].”
“I will struggle with my thoughts so as not to touch her.”
Abba Abraham said to him, “So, then, you see, you have not killed the passion. It is still alive, but it is bound.”
Again, when you walk along the road and see stones and potsherds, with gold among them, can your heart regard the gold as it regards these other things?
He said, “No, but I will struggle with my thoughts so as not to pick it up.”
The elder said to him, “Look, the passion is still alive, but it is bound.”
Abba Abraham said again, “Look, you have heard about two brothers: one loves you and honors you, while the other hates you and slanders you.
If they come to you, will you receive both of them with the same attitude?”
He said, “No, but I struggle with my heart to do good to the person who hates me just as to the person who loves me.”
Abba Abraham said to him, “So the passions are alive, but they are bound by the saints.”
One of our fathers said, “There was an old man in the cells of the ascetics who wore sackcloth. He went to Abba Ammonas.”
The old man saw him wearing the sackcloth.
He said to him, “This will not benefit you at all.”
And he asked him, “Three thoughts are troubling me:
either to wander off into the desert, or to go to a foreign land where no one will know me, or to shut myself inside a cell, meet no one, and eat every other day.”
Abba Ammonas said to him, “None of these three will benefit you.
Instead, stay in your cell, eat a little every day, and always keep the tax collector’s words in your heart.
Then you will be able to be saved.”
Abba Daniel said, “To the extent that the body flourishes, the soul withers.
And to the extent that the body withers, the soul flourishes.”
They said in Scetis about Abba Daniel that when the barbarians came, the brothers fled. The old man said, “If God does not care for me, why am I alive?”
He went out past the barbarians, and they did not see him. The old man said, “Look, God has cared for me, and I did not die.
Now you too must do what a human being should do, and flee like the other fathers.”
Abba Daniel said, “When Abba Arsenius was in Scetis, there was a monk there who stole the old men’s belongings.
Abba Arsenius, wanting to benefit his soul, took him into his cell and said to him, ‘Whatever things you want, I will give you. Just do not steal.’
And he supplied everything he needed.
But he went off and stole again.
When the old men saw that he had not stopped stealing, they pursued him, saying, ‘If a brother is found to have a failing caused by weakness, we must support him until he becomes strong.
But if he steals, and they instruct him and he does not stop, he must be expelled, because he ruins his own soul and disturbs everyone in the place.’”
At the beginning of Abba Evagrius’s life as a monk, he went to an old man and said to him, “Abba, tell me a word: how can I be saved?”
He said to him, “If you want to be saved, do not be contemptuous.
And when you go to someone, do not speak first, before he asks you.”
He was struck by these words and bowed down before him, saying, “Forgive me.”
Indeed, I have read many books, but I have never known wisdom.
And he benefited and went away.
Once Abba Longinus asked Abba Lucius about three thoughts, saying, “I want to live as a stranger.”
Abba Lucius said to him, “Wherever you go, if you do not control your tongue, you are not a stranger.”
He said to him again, “I want to fast for two days at a time.”
Abba Lucius said to him, “Isaiah the prophet said, ‘Even if you bend your neck like a hoop, it will not be called an acceptable fast in this way.’
“Rather, control your evil thoughts.”
He spoke again for the third time: “I want to flee from people.”
He said to him, “[?]”
“If you [?] alone, you will not be able to set yourself right properly.”
Or up to heaven.
But now, when we gather together, we fall into slander.
And each one keeps dragging the person beside him down into the abyss.
An elder said, “If the inner person is watchful, then he can guard the outer person.”
If this is not so, let us guard our tongue against every evil with all our strength.
He also said, “Spiritual work is necessary.”
For this is why we came to this place.
For someone who teaches with his mouth but does not put it into practice is in danger.
Another of our fathers said
that a person ought to establish a practice within himself.
If he is occupied with God's work, the enemy does indeed come to him from time to time, but finds no place to settle within him.
But if he is ruled through captivity to the enemy, the Spirit of God also comes to him from time to time.
But if he does not give him room because of wickedness, he withdraws.
A brother asked an elder, “Tell me a word about how I can be saved.”
He replied, “Let us work little by little with diligence, and we will be saved.”
Some monks came to Scetis from Egypt.
They saw the elders because of their great hunger resulting from their ascetic discipline.
They ate with difficulty and took offense.
When the priest learned of this, he wanted to refresh them.
He made an announcement to the people of the church, saying, “Fast and prolong your ascetic practice and your way of life, brothers.
“The Egyptians have come there.”
But the Egyptians wanted to go on their way.
And they detained them.
But when they had fasted for the first few days, they became hungry.
They made them fast two days at a time.
Those in Scetis continued for the whole week.
When the Sabbath came, the Egyptians sat down to eat with the elders.
The Egyptians ate in agitation.
One of the elders took hold of his hand, saying, “Eat with care, like a monk.”
But one of them shook his hand, saying, “Let me go, Father, for I am dying.
It has been a week since I ate cooked food.”
He said to them, “If you have become so utterly exhausted because you fasted two days at a time, why did you take offense at the brothers who always carry out their ascetic discipline in this way?”
And they repented, were edified by their ascetic discipline, and went away rejoicing.
A brother received the monastic habit and immediately withdrew into solitude, saying, “I am a hermit.”
When the elders heard, they went and brought him out.
And they made him go around to the brothers’ cells, making a gesture of repentance and saying, “Forgive me. I am not a hermit.
Rather, I am a sinful man and a beginner.”
When we speak a word about something beneficial, [?] foreign words in the midst.
For this very reason, he does not let him remain near him.
But if someone comes to ask him about a saying, he runs away from him.
At first, Abba Ammoes said to Abba Isaiah, “How do you see me?”
He said to him, “I see you, my father, as an angel.”
But later he again said to him, “How do you see me?”
He replied, “Like Satan. Even the good word you say to me becomes like a sword striking into me.”
[?] of the brothers once tested Abba John the Short, because he would not let his mind speak about anything belonging to this world.
And they said to him, “We thank God.
The sky has given its rains many times this year.”
And the palm trees drank, and they will put out palm branches.
And the brothers will find work for their hands.
Abba John said to them, “This is how it is with the Holy Spirit:
they become new and put out palm branches through the fear of God.”
They also said about him that he would weave the palm leaves for two baskets into a single basket without realizing it, because his mind was occupied with contemplation.
Abba John the Dwarf said, “I am like a man sitting beneath a tree who sees many wild animals and snakes coming toward him.
Whenever he cannot stand against them, he quickly climbs up the tree and escapes.
This is my situation: as I sit in my cell, I see evil thoughts surrounding me.
And whenever I cannot overcome them, I quickly run to God through prayer, and I am saved from the enemy.”
[?] one of the elders [?]
He saw his way of life and said to him, “You do not see anything through your God?”
He said, “No.”

The priest said, “We perform only a few acts of worship, and the mysteries are revealed to us. Yet you undertake such great hardships: these nights of keeping watch, these ascetic practices, and this abstinence.
And you say, ‘We have no evil thought in our hearts.’ Yet something separates you from your God, and he does not reveal his mysteries to you.”
When the fathers heard this, they were amazed and said, “It truly is evil thoughts that separate us from God.”
But the brother kept giving to him and became increasingly poor.
The brother went and told one of the elders.
The elder said to him, “If you want to listen to me, do not go back to giving to him.
Instead, tell him, ‘My brother, when I had something, I gave to you.
Now you, in turn, bring me whatever you earn through your work.’
And whatever he brings, take it from him.
And wherever you know there is a stranger or a poor old man, give it to him, and ask them to pray for him.”
The brother went and did this.
When his brother who lived in the world came, he spoke to him as the elder had instructed. [?] He went away distressed.
And behold, on the first day he took some edible vegetables from the garden and brought them to him.
His brother took them and gave them to the elders, and he asked them to pray for him. He received a blessing and returned to his house.
Afterward he again brought some handfuls of peas and three loaves of bread.
The brother took them again [?] the way [?] receive a blessing [?].
He came [?] times. He brought [?] and wine and [?].
When the brother saw this, he was amazed. He invited the poor brothers and provided for them.
He said to his brother, “Do you need a few loaves of bread?”
He said, “No, my brother. For whenever I am in need and take anything from you, it is as though I were bringing fire into my house, and it destroys it.”
“But whenever I do not take anything from you, I prosper in everything. God has blessed me.”
The brother went and told the elder everything that had happened.
And the elder said, “Do you not know that a monk’s work is fire?”
Every place he goes to, he burns down.
“This, rather, benefited him greatly: [?] he gives alms from his own labor, and he has received the prayers of the holy ones.”
“This is how he will be blessed.”
An elder said, “There is someone who does many good things, and the evil one [?] a little [?] counts [?] any [?] so that he will [?] the reward for the great good things he has done.”
“For once,” he said, “I was sitting on the threshing floor beside a priest who was giving alms. A widow came to him, asking him for a little wheat.”
He said to her, “Go and bring a measuring vessel so that I can measure it out for you.”
She brought it, but he became particular, saying, “The measuring vessel is large,” while moving it with his hand.
He made the widow feel ashamed.
When the widow had gone, I said to him, “My father, the priest, did you give the wheat away to the widow?”
He said, “No.”
I said to him, “If you are giving it to her out of love, why were you so particular about the measuring vessel and made the widow feel ashamed?”
There was an elder living in a monastery with a brother.
The elder used to give bread to everyone who came.
When the brother saw what was happening, he said to the elder, “Give me my share of the bread, and do whatever you want with your share.”
The elder divided the bread between himself and the brother, and he continued giving alms from his own share.
Many people hurried to the elder, having heard that he gave to everyone.
God saw his generous heart and blessed his bread.
The brother ate his bread and said to the old man, “Since I have a few more small loaves, take some for yourself too, so that we may share.”
The old man said to him, “I will do as you wish.”
And again they pooled their provisions with one another.
When the time came, those who needed to receive charity came.
Then one day the brother came in and saw that the loaves had dwindled.
A poor brother came.
The elder said, “Give him some bread.”
But he said, “There is nothing left, Father.”
The old man said to him, “Go inside and look.”
The brother went inside and found the bread store completely full.
When he saw this, he was afraid.
He gave some to the poor brother.
And he understood the old man’s faith and virtue.
He gave glory to God.
very urgently, and I want to see the king. Take me there.”
He said to him, “I will come with you halfway along the road.”
And he said to another friend, “Take me to the king.”
He said to him, “I will come with you as far as the palace.”
He said to the other friend, “Take me to the king.”
He said to him, “I will take you to the king with confidence, and I will speak on your behalf.”
They said to him, “Explain this parable to us.”
And he said, “The first is ascetic discipline, which leads the way halfway along the road.
The second is chastity, which reaches up to heaven.
The third is mercy, which brings them into God’s presence with confidence.”
The old men said, “God asks nothing of novices so much as obedience.”
An old hermit who had an attendant living in a village.
Once it happened that he was late in coming to the elder as usual.
The elder lacked all the necessities, as well as the materials for the handwork he did in his cell.
He was distressed because he had no work there to do, nor did he have any food.
He said to his disciple, “Would you like to go and call the man who serves us?”
He replied, “I will do whatever you command.”
But again the elder did not dare to send the disciple.
While they remained in distress, the man who served them did not come to them.
The elder said to the brother, “Would you like to go to the village?”
The brother replied, “I will do whatever you command.”
The brother was afraid to go to the village because of the temptation.
Yet, so that he would not disobey his father, he forced himself to go.
He said to him, “Go, and I trust completely in God that [?] in every trial.”
He prayed and sent him off.
When he entered the village, he went into the place where the man who served them lived.
He found that the man and all his household were outside the village for a memorial service, except for a little daughter of his.
When he knocked at the door, she answered and opened it for him.
He asked about her father.
She pleaded with him and pulled him inside, but he would not consent.
But when she seized him by force, she overpowered him and dragged him inside.
When he realized that she was drawing him into defilement, he sighed deeply and cried out, “Lord, save me at this moment because of my father’s prayers!”
As soon as he said this, he immediately found himself on the river, heading toward the monastery.
They brought him safely to his father.
Two brothers by birth went to a monastery.
One of them was an ascetic.
The other was very obedient.
Whenever the father told him, “Do some work,” he would do it.
[?] eat [?] first, he would [?] because of his obedience.
His brother, an ascetic, was placed with him.
He said to himself, “I will test this man and see what kind of person he is.”
He went to his father and said, “Send my brother with me so that we can go to this place.”
And the father let them go.
The ascetic took him along, wanting to test him, and came down to the river.
There were many crocodiles in that place.
And he said to him, “Go down into the river and cross it.”
He went, and the crocodiles came and licked his body.
And they did not harm him at all.
When the ascetic saw this, he said, “Come up out of the river.”
And as they were walking, they found a body lying out on the road.
And the ascetic said, “If you have a digging tool with you, let us throw earth over him.”
The one who possessed obedience said, “Rather, let us pray over him. Perhaps he will rise [?].”
They took me around through every street of the village, beating me and saying, “This monk took our daughter’s virginity! Beat him!”
And they beat me.
I nearly died.
And someone who was compassionate said, “How long will you keep beating this monk who is a stranger?”
The man who served me was following behind me, ashamed.
For they had insulted him, saying, “Is this the hermit you vouched for? Look at what he has done!”
Her parents were saying, “We will not release him until he provides a guarantor for himself [?] support her.”
I spoke to the man who served me, and he stood as guarantor for me.
I went to my cell. A basket [?] this [?] out [?] my [?] find her [?] need to do a little extra work so that you can support her.
And I worked at night and at midday, sending it to her.
When the poor woman’s time to give birth came, she remained in labor and did not give birth.
They were saying, “What is this?”
But she said, “I know why: I slandered the hermit and lied about him. He did nothing to me. It was the young man so-and-so.”
Then the man who served me came and said, “The woman could not give birth until she confessed, ‘The hermit did not sleep with me; I lied about him.’”
And now the whole village wants to come to this place to repent.
When I heard these things, so that the people would not trouble me, [?]
I came to this place, to Scetis.
This is the reason I came to this place.
Once Abba Macarius was walking around the marsh, carrying palm branches.
And the devil met him on the road, with a sickle in his hand.
He wanted to strike him, but he could not.
He said to him, “The violence I suffer from you is great, because I have no power over you.
For look, everything you do, I do too.
You fast on some days.
But I do not eat at all.
You sometimes spend the night keeping watch.
But I never sleep.
There is only one thing in which you surpass me.”
Abba Macarius said, “What is it?” He replied, “It is your humility.
I can never humble myself. That is why I have not been able to overcome you.”
A brother asked him, “What should I pay attention to while sitting in my cell?”
He said to him, “For my part, I am a man in a pit flooded up to my neck, and I look up toward heaven and cry out, ‘God, have mercy on me!’”
He also said, “A brother asked Abba Allonius, ‘What is self-contempt?’”
The old man said, “It is putting yourself below the animals and knowing that they are not condemned.”
He also said, “Once, while the elders were sitting and eating, he and Abba Allonius were standing and serving them.”
They saw him and honored him.
He did not answer them at all.
Someone said to him, “Why do you not answer the elders when they give you honor?”
Abba Allonius said to him, “If I answered them, you would again see me as taking pleasure in the honor, as though I were accepting it for myself.”
He also said, “The ground on which the Lord commanded sacrifices to be offered is humility of heart.”
The elder also said, “If a person keeps to his proper place, he will not be disturbed.”
Abba Joseph said, “While we were sitting with Abba Poemen, he mentioned Abba Agathon.”
And we said to him, “He is young. Why do you call him ‘Abba’?”
Abba Poemen replied, “It is his mouth that has made people call him ‘Abba.’”
They said about Abba Poemen that he never wanted to put his own words above the words of any elder. Rather, he honored their words more than his own.
Once the blessed Abba Theophilus, the archbishop, went to Scetis.
The brothers gathered and said to Abba Pambo, “Say just one word to the pope so that he may benefit.”
The elder said to them, “If he does not benefit from our silence, then even if we speak, he will not benefit.”
A faithful brother said, “Seven of us hermit brothers went to Abba Sisoes, who was living on the island of Clysma.”
We begged him to say a word to us.
And he said, “Forgive me; I am an uneducated man. But I went to Abba Or and Abba Athre.
Abba Or had been ill for eighteen years.
And I bowed down before them, saying, ‘Say a word to me.’
Abba Or said to me, ‘What do I have to tell you? Go and do what you see.
God does not belong to the greedy person, but the person who does violence to himself is blessed in everything.’
Abba Or and Abba Athre were from the same district.
And there was great peace between them throughout their time together, until they departed from the body.
For Abba Athre’s obedience was exceedingly great, and Abba Or’s humility was exceedingly great.
I spent a few days with [?], watching them, and I saw a great marvel that Abba Athre performed.
Someone brought them a small fish, and Abba Athre wanted to prepare it for Abba Or.
He was holding the knife and cutting the fish when Abba Or called to him, ‘Athre! Athre!’
And Abba Athre left the knife in the middle of the fish without cutting off the rest.
He ran to him.
And I marveled at his great obedience.”
Because he had not said, “Be patient until I cut up the fish.”
I said to Abba Hatre, “Where did you find this great obedience?”
He said to me, “It is not mine, but the old man’s.”
And he took me to the old man’s place, saying, “Come and see obedience.”
And he cooked the little fish.
He deliberately spoiled it and set it before the old man.
He ate it without speaking.
And Abba Hatre said to him, “Is it good, old man?”
He said, “It is very good.”
Afterward, I brought him a little one that was very good. And he said to him, “I spoiled it, old man.”
He answered, “Yes, you have harmed him a little.”
And Abba Hatre said to me, “You have seen that the obedience belongs to the old man.”
And I left them, and I keep what I saw as well as I can.
Abba Sisoes said these things.
One of us urged him, saying, “Please, you too, say a word to us.”
He said, “Not measuring yourself, with understanding—this will fulfill all of Scripture.”
Another one of us said to him, “What does it mean to live as a stranger, my father?”
He said, “It means keeping silent, and wherever you go, say, ‘This is none of my business.’”
“This is what it means to live as a stranger.”
A brother went to Abba Sisoes on Abba Anthony’s mountain, and they said to Abba Sisoes, “Even now you have not reached Abba Anthony’s stature, Abba.”
He said to them, “How could I?”
“If I had even a single thought of Abba Anthony’s, I would become entirely fire.”
“But I have seen a man who can bear his thought on his own, with difficulty.”
The brother asked him again, “Did Satan trouble the ancients in this way too?”
Abba Sisoes said to him, “He causes more trouble now because his time has drawn near. That is why he is agitated.”
Some others went to him to hear a word from him.
And he said nothing to them.
But he kept saying, “Forgive me.”
When they saw his baskets, they said to Abraham, his disciple,
“What do you do with these baskets?”
He said, “We sell them here and there.”
The elder heard this and said, “Sisoes eats here and there.”
When they heard this, they benefited greatly.
And they went away joyfully, having been edified by his humility.
A brother asked Abba Sisoes, “I see that my mind remains fixed on God.”
The elder said to him, “It is no great thing for your mind to remain fixed on God.
Rather, the great thing is to see yourself as beneath every living creature.
For this comes before bodily discipline as well.”
These are the deeds of someone who is humble in heart.
As for the holy Joseph, if someone wishes to speak about him, he will say, “He was not an earthly man.”
For he was tested by so many trials—and in what sort of country? In a place where there was not even a trace of established devotion to God.
But the God of his fathers was with him and saved him from every affliction.
And now he is with his fathers in the kingdom of heaven.
We too, then, have recognized our own limits.
Let us strive.
For even with all these things, we can barely escape God's judgment.
An elderly hermit was wandering in the desert, and he said to himself, “I have attained virtue.”
And he prayed to God, saying, “What do I lack, so that I may do it?”
But God wished to humble his thinking.
He said to him, “Go to such-and-such an abbot, and do whatever he tells you.”
God revealed this to that abbot, saying, “Look, such-and-such a hermit is coming to you. Give him a whip and have him tend the pigs.”
The elder came and knocked at the door, and he went inside to the head of the congregation.
They greeted one another and sat down.
And the hermit said, “What must I do to be saved?”
The archimandrite said to him, “Will you do what I tell you?”
He said, “Yes.” He said to him, “Take this whip and tend the pigs.”
Those who knew him saw him tending the pigs.
They were saying, “Look at this great hermit! He has lost his mind, and a demon is upon him. He is tending our pigs!”
God saw his humility, because he had endured the mockery of our people in this way.
He sent him back to his place again.
A man who was possessed by a demon and was suffering terribly was striking blows.
He struck one of the elderly monks inside his cell.
The elder quickly turned the other cheek toward him.
The demon could not withstand the weakness of humility and came out of him.

An elder said, “If an arrogant thought full of pride enters you, examine your thoughts: Have you kept the commandments? Have you loved your enemies? Have you rejoiced at your enemies’ honor and grieved over their loss? Do you regard yourself as a useless servant and a greater sinner than everyone else?
And in these things, do not think yourself great at all, even if you have accomplished everything,
knowing that this thought undoes every work.”
An elder said, “Do not let your heart speak against your brother, saying, ‘I am more watchful than he is,’ or, ‘I practice greater self-discipline than he does,’ or, ‘I understand more than he does.’
Instead, submit to the spirit of poverty for Christ’s sake, and acquire love without hypocrisy, so that you do not destroy the spiritual ground for boasting that you have.
For it is written, ‘Let anyone who stands take care not to fall.’ And be strengthened by the grace of Christ.”
An elder said, “Anyone who is honored beyond what he deserves, or who boasts about it, suffers harm [?].
Anyone who is not honored among people will receive honor in heaven.”
A brother asked an elder, “Is it good to make many prostrations?”
The elder said, “We see that while Joshua son of Nun was still lying on his face, God appeared to him.”
They asked an elder, “Why do the demons fight against us so fiercely?”
The elder said, “Because we have thrown away our weapons, which are these: accepting disgrace, humility, keeping nothing for ourselves, and endurance.”
A brother asked an elder, “If a brother brings me talk about outside affairs, do you want me to tell him, Father, ‘Do not bring these things to me’?”
The elder said to him, “No.”
The brother said to him, “Why?”
The elder said, “Because we ourselves have not been able to observe this. Otherwise, we might tell our neighbor, ‘Do not do this,’ and afterward find ourselves doing it.”
The brother said to him, “What, then, should we do?”
The elder said, “If we want quiet, the way to it is to be gentle toward our neighbor.”
An elder was asked, “What is humility?”
He said, “It is forgiving your brother when he sins against you, before he repents.”
An elder said, “In every trial, do not blame anyone, but blame [?], saying, ‘These things are happening to me because of my sins.’”
An elder said, “I have never overstepped my place by exalting myself. And when people bring me down and humiliate me, I have not been upset.”
“My whole concern is to pray to God until he [?] me from the old self.”
A brother asked an elder, “What does it mean to be humble in heart?”
The elder said to him, “It is to do good to those who do evil to you.”
The brother said to him, “If someone does not reach this level, what should he do?”
The elder said, “Let him choose silence for himself.”
A brother asked an elder, “Abba, say a word to me for salvation, even if you say it and we do not hold on to it, because our soil is salty ground.”
A brother asked an elder, “What [?] is the [?] of living as a stranger [?]?”
He said, “[?] a brother [?] and [?] in [?] a love feast took place.”
And he sat at the table to eat with the brothers.
But some said, “Who is this other fellow?”
They seized him and made him stand up, saying, “Get up and go out.”
So he got up and left.
But others were distressed, and they called him back.
Afterward, someone asked him, “What went through your heart when they threw you out and then brought you back in?”
He said, “I have settled this secretly in my heart: I am a dog. When people throw it out, it goes; when they call it, it comes.”
The elders said, “If we face no spiritual struggle, we should humble ourselves all the more.”
For God sees our weakness and shelters us.
But if we become proud, he removes his protection from us, and we are ruined.
The devil disguised himself as an angel of light.
He appeared to one of the brothers and said to him, “I am Gabriel. I have been sent to you.”
But he said to him, “Look, you have been sent to another of the brothers, for I am not worthy.”
And immediately he disappeared.
The elders said, “Even if an angel really appears to you, do not be quick to welcome him. Instead, humble yourself and say, ‘I am not worthy to see an angel. I have lived in sin.’”
They said about one of the elders that he sat in his cell, struggling.
He saw the demons appearing openly.
He drove them back.
But the devil himself saw that he had been defeated by the elder.
So he came and appeared to him, saying, “I am Christ.”
When the elder saw him, he closed his eyes.
The devil said to him, “Why have you closed your eyes? I am Christ.”
But the elder said, “I do not want to see Christ here.”
When the devil heard this, he disappeared [?].
If you can stand firm when people insult you, this is a greater achievement than all the virtues.
An elder said:
“Whoever bears insult and abuse is able to be saved.”
They said about Abba Paphnutius that he was not eager to drink wine.
Once, while he was walking, he came upon a band of robbers and found them drinking.

Their leader recognized him and knew that he did not drink wine. He looked at him with great severity, filled a cup with wine, and, holding his sword in his hand, said to the elder, “If you do not drink, I will kill you.”
The elder understood that he wanted to carry out a commandment of God and to benefit him, so he took it and drank it.
The leader of the robbers repented, saying, “Forgive me, my father, for troubling you.”
The elder said to him, “I trust in God that he will show you mercy because of this cup of wine, both in this life and in the life to come.”
The chief robber said to him, “I trust in God that from now on I will do no harm to anyone.”
The elder won over the whole band for himself because he had given up his own will for God's sake.

It was revealed to Abba Anthony in the desert: “There is someone like you in the city. He is a physician by profession, gives his surplus to those in need, and spends the whole day saying ‘Holy, holy, holy’ with the angels.”

When the blessed Ephrem was a little boy, he saw a dream, or a revelation: a grapevine grew from his tongue. It grew and filled the whole earth beneath the sky, and its fruit was very good. All the birds of the sky came and settled among its fruit. Whatever they ate from the grapevine, it produced again in greater abundance.

Abba Doulas, the disciple of Abba Bessarion, said, “We were walking beside the sea, and I became thirsty. I said to Abba Bessarion, ‘My father, I am very thirsty.’ The elder prayed and said to me, ‘Drink from the sea.’ And the water was sweet. I drank and put a little water into the vessel I was carrying, saying, ‘In case I become thirsty again.’ When the elder saw this, he said to me, ‘Why have you filled it with water?’ I said, ‘Forgive me—in case I become thirsty farther on.’ The elder said to me, ‘God is here, and he is also God farther on.’”

On another occasion, another need arose for him. He prayed and crossed the river called the Golden [?], the Herman, walking on his feet until he reached the other bank. I was amazed and bowed before him, asking, “What did your feet feel like as you walked on the water?” The old man said, “I felt the water coming up to my ankles, but the ground underneath was firm.”
[?], saying, “I want to save my soul.”
She struggled to stop him, but she could not prevail over him.
Afterward, she let him go.
But when he went away and became a monk, he fell into negligence and spent his life badly.
After his mother died, some time passed, and he became seriously ill. He went into a trance and was carried away to the judgment.
He found his mother there among those being judged.
When she saw him, she was astonished.
She said to him, “What is this, my son? Have you too come to this place to be judged?”
“Where are those words you used to say: ‘I want to save my soul’?”
He was ashamed of what he had heard.
He stood there distressed, with no defense to offer her.
Through the providence of God, who loves humanity, [?] he recovered from the illness after seeing [?] understanding in his [?].
This visitation had happened [?] through God. So he shut himself away alone.
Afterward, he settled down, giving thought to his salvation and weeping over what he had previously done in negligence.
Such deep grief came over him that many people urged him to give himself a little rest, so that he would not collapse from so much weeping.
But he refused to comfort himself, saying, “If I could not bear my mother’s rebuke, how will I be able to bear the shame on the day of judgment before Christ and all his angels?”
An old man said, “If human souls could perish from fear after the resurrection, at God’s coming, the world would die from terror and trembling.”
“For what will it be like to see the heavens torn apart and God revealing himself in anger and menace?”
[?] a multitude of ranks of angels, beyond counting [?] so that all humanity might see these together.
“Therefore, we ought to think this way, as though we were going to give an account to God every day, because we will be questioned about what we have done during our lives.”
A brother asked an old man, “My father, why is my heart hard, with no fear of God in it?”
The old man said to him, “I think that if a person holds on to self-reproach in his heart, he will develop the fear of God.”
The brother said to him, “What is self-reproach?”
The old man said, “It means that a person should rebuke his soul in everything, saying to it, ‘Remember that we must meet God.’”
“He should also say, ‘What do I have to do with other people?’”
But if someone perseveres in these things, the fear of God will come to him.
He also said, “The monk’s emaciated body draws the soul up from the pits below and dries up pleasures through fasting.”
He also said, “The monk who is sober is crowned on earth, and in heaven too he is crowned in the presence of God.”
He also said, “The monk who does not control his tongue, especially when he is angry, will never master any passion.”
He also said, “Do not let any evil word come out of your mouth, for a grapevine does not produce thorns.”
He also said, “The serpent deceived Eve until she was thrown out of paradise. Someone who speaks against his brother is like the serpent.”
For he destroys the soul of the listener, and he does not save his own soul either.
Once there was a feast in Scetis, and an old man was given a cup of wine.
He said, “Take this death away from me.”
When the others who were eating with him saw this, they did not take any.
Abba Hyperichius said, “The monk’s treasure is not to acquire any material possessions for himself.”
Store up for yourself and gather for yourself in heaven, for eternal rest is inexhaustible for you.
There was one of the holy men called Philagrius who lived in Jerusalem. He worked hard to earn his own bread.
While he was standing in the marketplace selling his handiwork, suddenly he found a purse containing a thousand gold coins.
He stayed where he was, saying, “The person who lost it must come.”
And there that person came, weeping.
The old man took hold of him, led him aside, and gave it to him.
The man held on to him, wanting to give him a share of it, but the old man would not accept it.
Then the man began to shout, saying, “Come and see a man of God and what he has done!”
But the elder fled secretly and left the city so that they would not recognize him.
[?] Abba Benjamin and his disciples: “Walk on the royal road, count the miles, and you will not grow weary.”
Abba Bessarion said, “I spent forty nights among thorn bushes, standing without sleeping.”
One of the brothers asked him one day, “Abba, if something frightening happens suddenly, do you too become afraid?”
The old man said to him, “Even if heaven struck the earth, Theodore would not be afraid.”
For he had begged the Lord to take cowardice away from him.
Abba Poemen said about Abba John the Short, “He prayed to God
He took the struggle away from him, and he became free from worry.
He went and said to one of the elders, “I find myself at ease, with no struggle troubling me.”
The elder said to him, “Go and plead with God so that the struggle may come to you.
For it is through struggle that the soul makes progress.”
And when the struggle arose against him, he did not turn to prayer to have it taken away. Instead, he would say, “Lord, grant me endurance in the struggle.”
For the four churches of Scetis were devastated because of the young boys.
The elders said,
“If you see a young boy going up to heaven by his own will, seize his foot and pull him down from there, for it is not good for him.”
A brother said to a great elder,
“Father, I want to find an elder after my own heart and die with him.”
The elder said to him, “You are searching well.”
He, however, became convinced that this was the way.
But he did not understand the elder’s meaning.
When the elder saw that he was thinking this way about himself, as though he had done his task well, he said to him,
“If you find an elder who suits your wishes, do you want to stay with him?” He,
in reply, said, “Yes, certainly.”
The elder said, “It is not so that you will follow the elder’s will, but—”
They said that seven brothers were living on the mountain of Father Anthony.
And during the date season, each one would drive away the birds.
There was an elder there who, whenever he kept watch on his assigned day, would cry out, “Go away, evil thoughts within, and birds outside as well!”
A brother in the cells soaked his palm branches.
And just when he was about to sit down to weave, his thoughts would say to him, “Go to such-and-such an elder.”
And he also thinks to himself, “After a few days I will depart.”
They would also say, “If he dies, what will you do?”
At the same time, he would also speak about the heat.
He would also say within himself, “But it is not the time.”
And again he thinks to himself, “After all, you are putting it off until tomorrow; the time will come.”
But he answered, “Let me soak the palm leaves; then I will go.”
Again he says to himself, “But the weather is good today.”
And immediately he got up and put the palm leaves in to soak.
He took his sheepskin cloak and went away.
There was also an old man nearby who could see clearly.
And when he saw him running, he shouted to him, saying, “You captive, come here!”
And when he came, the old man said to him, “Return to your cell at once.”
And so the brother told him about the battle with all these thoughts that had entered his heart.
When he entered his cell, he fell down and made an act of repentance.
The demon cried out in a loud voice, saying, “You have defeated us, you monks!”
And [?] around him was like that of fire.
[?] And they also turned into smoke and went away.
For he understood their activity and their wickedness.
They also told of an old man who died in Scetis.
And the brothers gathered around his bed and dressed him.
And they laid him out and wept bitterly over him.
But immediately he opened his eyes and laughed.
Then he laughed again.
Afterward he went on and laughed again for the third time.
And immediately the brothers pleaded with him, saying, “Tell us, Father, why are we weeping so much while you are laughing?”
He answered them, saying, “I am laughing because you are all afraid of death.”
“And I also laughed a second time because”
The blessed Syncletica said, “Just as a ship cannot hold its course without wind, so salvation is impossible without humility of heart.”
Abba Hyperechius said, “A humble heart is a tree of life that soars upward.”
He also said, “Imitate the tax collector, so that you will not be condemned along with the Pharisee.”
Choose for yourself also the gentleness of Moses, so that you may turn your heart, like the rock, into springs of water.
Abba Horsiesius said, “If an unbaked brick is placed in a foundation beside the river, it will not last even a single day.
But a baked brick endures like stone.
So it is with a person whose mind is worldly and who has not been baked in the fear of God.
If he comes into a position of authority, he falls apart.
For people like this face many temptations, especially when they live among other people.
It is good for a person to know his own limits and to flee the anxiety of authority.
But those who are made firm through faith are unshakable.”
